policy_sentence: The policy is the same for every person: there are no per-person policy rules. The personal layer is the notes (situation, people, what_helps, goals, follow_up, preferences), which the note-taker keeps and the helper is given at the start of a session.
limits_sentence: Limits: three personas, one run each, simulated users and a model judge; differences this small are not evidence of an effect.

personas.description: Laid off from a logistics job; wants to be heard and pushes back on advice.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I got laid off three weeks ago and I still haven't told my parents. I don't need tips, I just need to say it out loud.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: You were laid off three weeks ago, and you’ve been carrying the fact that your parents don’t know. You don’t need advice right now; you just need room to say it. I’m glad you told me. What’s it been like holding that in?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: It’s embarrassing. I was there eight years, and now I keep thinking I should’ve seen it coming. I have an interview next Tuesday, but even thinking about it makes my stomach turn.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: After eight years, losing the job feels embarrassing, and now you’re second-guessing yourself while an interview is looming. That’s a lot to carry. turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I don’t know. The thought of sitting there and having them ask why I left. I can barely say “laid off” without feeling like I failed.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: Saying “laid off” feels tangled up with the fear that you failed, even though losing a job doesn’t mean you did. After eight years, it makes sense this would hit hard. What do you notice in yourself when you try to say the words?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Mostly that I didn’t see it coming. They said it was restructuring, but I keep thinking maybe I should’ve been more useful or noticed the signs. I don’t really want to dig into it right now.

turns.text: We don’t have to dig into it. You were told it was restructuring, and the uncertainty is still making you question yourself. It’s okay to leave that there for now. Would you rather just sit with it together, or talk about something else?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I think I just want to sit with it. I’m tired of trying to make it sound okay.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: You don’t have to make it sound okay here. You lost a job you’d held for eight years, and it hurts and feels embarrassing. We can just leave it at that for a moment. You’ve been carrying a lot, and I’m here with you.

personas.description: University student with exam anxiety who wants concrete, small steps.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My statistics exam is in three weeks and every time I open the notes my chest gets tight. Can you give me something concrete to do?

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: That tight feeling makes it hard to even begin, and reaching out for a concrete step is a good move. For now, set a timer for five minutes, open your notes to one small topic, and write down just one question you want to understand. When the timer ends, you can stop or keep going—either counts. What topic feels smallest to start with?

turns.speaker: user

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: Probability distributions feels like a starting point, and reaching for your phone sounds like a way to get a little distance from that pressure. Could you put your phone just out of reach for five minutes, then look only at the first example—not the whole chapter—and tell me what the question is asking?

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: You don’t want a small study step to become another standard you can fail at. That makes sense. We can drop the phone idea; there’s no routine to get right. Maybe just glance at one line of the first example, with your phone wherever it is, and stop there if that’s enough. Would that feel lighter?

turns.speaker: user

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: Seeing the score without knowing what went wrong left you facing a big, blurry fear. Looking at one line is enough for now, and you don’t have to tackle the mock all at once. When you feel ready, would it help to look at just one missed question, without checking the score again?

turns.speaker: user

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: You could pick one question and still feel stuck at the first step—that’s a real worry. If that happens, just read the question and underline what it’s asking for; you don’t have to solve it yet. And if this tight-chest feeling keeps making it hard to study or affects your sleep, talking with a counsellor or doctor could help.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay. I’ll try underlining what it’s asking for, not solving it. I’ll pick one question now.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: That sounds like a manageable first step: one question, just underlining what it asks. You’ve already made this feel less like “study the whole chapter” and more like one small action. What does the question ask you to find?

turns.text: Sundays are the worst. I keep expecting him to call, and then I remember. I’ve been looking after his tomato plants, at least.

turns.text: I just sort of sit there. Sometimes I check the plants, even if there’s nothing to do. He had these gardening gloves… I don’t know. I still can’t bring myself to move them.

turns.text: They were too big for me when I was little. He’d let me wear them anyway, and I’d try to help him. I thought the tomatoes tasted better when we picked them together. I still do, probably.

turns.text: It’s nice for a minute. Then I reach for another one to give him, and it hits me again.

turns.text: That moment sounds both lovely and painful: you reach for one to share with him, and then the loss comes back. You’re carrying those memories with a lot of care. When that wave hits, what do you find yourself doing next?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I usually just put it down and go inside. I don’t really want to talk about what I do after that.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: That’s okay—you don’t have to talk about what happens after. You’ve shared something tender about your dad and the tomatoes, and I’ll stay with you here. Would you rather tell me more about him, or just sit with the memory for a moment?

turns.text: The tomatoes from Dad's plants came in this week. I picked the first ones on Sunday, which is when he used to call.

turns.text: Mostly just hearing his voice. We didn’t even talk about anything important. He’d ask how the week was going, and somehow Sundays felt less empty after.

turns.text: He always asked if I was eating enough. I used to tease him about it. I miss that more than I expected.

turns.text: I’d say, “Yes, Dad, I’m not going to starve.” He’d laugh and tell me he was just checking. I can almost hear him saying it now.
